Q: AWS IAM Authentication on DB level A:

You can set up privileges in your database using PostgreSQL roles.

Grant privileges for a particular database in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL: Give all permissions to a user on a PostgreSQL database

These statements are similar to standard MySQL grants like GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON mydb.* TO 'myuser'@'localhost';. PostgreSQL consists of clusters (not the replication kind), containing databases, containing schemas, which contain tables, whereas many other database systems have databases which contain tables. The public schema is used by default, according to the search_path.

What a cluster. But this adds some versatility, where a single instance of PostgreSQL has a lot of hierarchical structure.

Prior to PostgreSQL 15, all users had CREATE privileges on the public schema.

This simulates the situation where schemas are not available at all, giving a smooth transition from the non-schema-aware world. However, this is never a secure pattern. It is acceptable only when the database has a single user or a few mutually-trusting users. In databases upgraded from PostgreSQL 14 or earlier, this is the default.

Schemas: Usage Patterns
PostgreSQL Documentation

It's understandable why they re-thought this.

With RDS, the users, schema, and SQL-layer setup are internal to your application code. This is unlike DynamoDB, where Tables are first class citizens in AWS. With that said, there are some standard solutions that allow you to bake this setup into your infrastructure, so that you are creating and configuring your database for your application.

Using IAM with RDS

IAM policies may be created to allow database-level access to specific users.

Creating and using an IAM policy for IAM database access
Amazon RDS Documentation

The Amazon Resource Name is formatted as follows:

arn:aws:rds-db:region:account-id:dbuser:DbiResourceId/db-user-name

To use this policy, create a corresponding database user and enable IAM authentication from within your database.

Creating a database account using IAM authentication
Amazon RDS Documentation

In PostgreSQL:

CREATE USER db_userx; 
GRANT rds_iam TO db_userx;

Setting up your database

How will you run the SQL statements to create a user and assign privileges?

Here you have some options depending on how you will be deploying your application.

CloudFormation

If your deployment is based on CloudFormation, the ideal way to handle this type of application-layer setup is to create a Custom Resource in CloudFormation that is able to perform this setup and inform CloudFormation of its lifecycle. This is simply a Lambda function that turns your deployment step into a CloudFormation-aware resource.

Lambda-backed custom resources
AWS CloudFormation Documentation

(ironically, the example creates a "delay mechanism" in Lambda)

In your case, you would create a Lambda function that runs SQL statements to set up your database. The Lambda function DependsOn an RDS resource returning a MasterUserSecret that can be passed in to your Lambda function's environment to connect to the database. You can also specify your own password for the master user. This gives Lambda a full-privilege user only for setup.

You would add your custom database setup resource to your application's DependsOn so that this initialization task runs before your application is launched.

CI/CD

If you are using some other deployment or orchestration technology, you would add a step that depends on the RDS instance creation and uses the MasterUserSecret to connect to the database for initial setup.

This could be a shell script that runs a .sql file containing all of the setup, deployment code written in a programming language using the AWS SDK, or user data passed into an EC2 instance.

The CI/CD technology could also be responsible for managing your secrets in a way you define, providing its own password to the RDS instance on creation.

User Data

The simplest solution is to add a user data script to your EC2 instance that runs the SQL statements at launch before it kicks off your application. This is less integrated into your infrastructure, and makes it less obvious when this initialization has succeeded. Here, a shell script retrieves the MasterUserSecret from the AWS CLI and connects to the database from the command line. Probably will require more IF EXISTS type statements, unless the database is guaranteed to only exist for the lifetime of the instance.

Now you have a production-ready user that you can dynamically connect to with IAM authentication.

Using IAM roles in your application

When you create an AWS resource and attach an IAM role, your application code connects using the AWS SDK and is automatically made aware of the role in the instance metadata.

IAM Roles for Amazon EC2
Amazon EC2 Documentation

Similarly, application code in Lambda may assume an execution role to gain IAM-based privileges.

As you have found in the linked tutorial, AWS SDKs allow you to generate authentication tokens that grant access to a database from your application.

This section of the RDS documentation has examples of using the AWS SDK in many programming languages:

Connecting to your DB instance using IAM authentication

Q: How do we deal with partially labelled data in Classification problems A:

This is usually handled as a semi-supervised learning problem.

If only part of your dataset has labels, you have a few options:

  1. Train only on labelled data
    Ignore the unlabelled samples and train a normal supervised classifier.

  2. Use semi-supervised learning
    Use both labelled and unlabelled data. For example, train on labelled data, then use the model to predict labels for unlabelled data.

  3. Pseudo-labelling
    Predict labels for unlabelled samples and add only high-confidence predictions back into training.

  4. Label propagation / consistency training
    Useful when similar samples are expected to have similar labels.

Important point:
Do not treat missing labels as class 0 or negative labels unless that is actually true.

For multi-label classification, missing label usually means unknown, not negative. In that case, you should mask unknown labels during loss calculation.

Q: How to read the value of a widget's padding option A:

padding is being returned as Tk distance objects rather than plain Python integers.

Tkinter/ttk internally stores geometry-related values (padding, width, etc.) as Tcl/Tk screen distances, so tkinter preserves them as Tcl objects instead of automatically converting them to int.

Your code is fine — you just need to convert them explicitly if you want normal Python integers:

padding = tuple(map(int, label.configure("padding")[-1]))

print(padding)
# (100, 50)

You can also access them through the widget option directly:

x, y = label["padding"]

print(int(x), int(y))

The reason this happens is that Tk distances are not limited to raw pixels. Values like these are also valid:


label.configure(padding=("2c", "1c"))

So tkinter cannot always assume the values should immediately become integers.

Q: Why do you include the .h file in the .cpp file and not the other way around? A:

why does #include "example.h" in main.cpp allow that file to access the function definition in example.cpp?

It doesn't. The header only provides the declaration of the function. The compiler is satisfied to merely know that the function exists and the arguments all line up (or can be converted to something that lines up).

After the compiler is done, along comes the linker to make sure everything that was used is defined in one of the compiled object files and then put the compiled objects together into an executable or dynamically-linkable library.

Handy reading: How does the compilation/linking process work?

Related reading: Why does C++ need a separate header file?

Side note: Careful with "prepend". The included header is not prepended. The #include directive is replaced with the contents of the named file. This can become important for later when you have multiple #include statements and headers that include other headers.
